quotes.text: The lead track, "I'm Sorry and I Love You," full of piano and falsetto, is ostensibly a love song, but it seems to be an overarching (but non-specific) apology – the first line, in fact, is "I remember you before you hated me."

There's an unevenness to the album, too. Many tracks seem to border on home demos, where others are full-band numbers – apparently, the album was culled largely from the three records that Adams was supposed to have released in 2019 before, well, you know.

"Birmingham" is a piano-driven rocker. "Poison & Pain" finds Adams acknowledging at least some of his issues – "My demons got so bored of dreamin'/My demons, alcohol and freedom." It's a pretty tune, with an almost innocent trip back to a time when booze was his biggest problem.

Perhaps an album dropped a couple weeks before Christmas isn't the place to address what he's accused of – and what he DID – but it still feels odd to have no acknowledgement from someone who's written exhaustively of seemingly every emotion he's ever experienced.
The records cover a wide stylistic territory from Americana to '80s-inspired punk rock, they're all very good, and this should be a crowning achievement for generational songwriting talent.

He released 13 full-length records between 2000 and 2011, not counting side projects and his work producing others' albums, and not every record he released was a solid effort. But despite the heavy output, flashes of songwriting genius were still a regular occurrence on every record.

Described by Adams on his Twitter page (since advance copies and press kits were not made available) as "the soundtrack to a movie from 1984 that exists only in my soul," Big Colors is, indeed, a whole mess of shimmery guitars, synth, and songs about rain and longing.

And it does, at times, feel cinematic. "It's So Quiet, It's Loud" is one of a few tunes that features strings. "Power," all choppy guitars and distorted vocals, could score a crazy foot chase scene through some 80s version of a postmodern decaying cityscape.
It's good. It feels like a logical successor to 2017's Prisoner. And it's a much more satisfying, cohesive listen than Wednesdays. Adams' "soundtrack from 1984" goal is met.
If Chris does anything, it proves that Ryan Adams remains one of great American rock songwriters in the tradition of Tom Petty and John Mellencamp.

this time out Adams delivers a lengthy 18 song collection marked by rootsy Americana rockers and numerous ballads that display his natural way with a melodic hook and some catchy, often colorful words.
Ryan moves back and forth with bold guitar rockers, like "Aching for More" and the rollicking "So Helpless," and a variety of acoustic ballads and slower, brooding rockers.

for all the emotions Adams wears on his song's sleeves, for all the anguish and longing, there's little here that will answer the questions raised by the allegations against him, just lots of semi-poetic wondering set to great guitar sounds and melodic hooks that linger in your memory long after you've stopped listening.
Chris is another fine example of the exemplary songwriting and recording that has made a significant number of his nearly 20 albums feel like pure rock & roll gold.
